newsitem.title: SPAIN: Dancing bishops, convicts rock at Madrid carnival.
newsitem.headline: Dancing bishops, convicts rock at Madrid carnival.

text.p: Dancing bishops, convicts and giant condoms mixed in an orgy of colour, glitter and feathers in Madrid on Saturday night as its annual carnival reached its climax.
Decked in their gaudiest attire, thousands of revellers strutted, paraded and boozed to the sound of drums, whistles and techno music to celebrate the countdown to Lent.

The annual procession of hundreds of dancers and glittering floats bounced its way through the city culminating in the central Plaza Mayor square where judges announced the parade winner, a recreation of the opera "Aida".
But the festivities did not stop there for most. Street parties sprang up around the city and nightclubs throbbed well into Sunday morning.
A select few made their way to the Bellas Artes club for the illustrious masked ball which opened its doors to transvestite nuns and festive priests.
But tickets were expensive and hard to come by, and two dejected revellers posing as gossiping housewives at their window sills heckled and teased ticket holders for their opulence as they entered.
However, Madrid was not the only city in Spain bursting into action.

On the Canary island of Tenerife, giant floats and dancing girls wearing little more than tangas and a few feathers rocked to the beat of samba music in a similar fashion to the legendary Rio carnival.
In Cadiz, celebrations centred around the annual ditty competition in which groups of singers performed ditties satirising politicians, the Royal family and celebrities.
Apart from the religious excuse for the carnivals, partygoers said they held added meaning for Spaniards, reminding them of the luxury of freedom since General Francisco Franco died in 1975.
"This wasn't allowed during Franco's time so now we go wild," said Emiliano Gironella, dressed as a shaggy dog at the Bellas Artes ball.
Carnivals were prohibited by the Franco regime because of their licentiousness and frivolity.

Carnival celebrations officially come to an end on Ash Wednesday with the Burial of the Sardine, in which a sardine representing winter is escorted around town in a tiny coffin before being ritually buried.
Municipal sources estimated around 100,000 people gathered to watch Madrid's parade.
